title: Consequences of chronic ketamine self-administration upon neurocognitive function and psychological wellbeing: A 1-year longitudinal study

claims.statement: In people who used ketamine frequently, the evidence is insufficient to say whether lower memory and thinking scores fade after they cut down or stop, and the question is contested. People who had stopped scored no lower than people who did not use ketamine: 30 people abstinent for at least a month (a mean of 344 days, range 120 to 2980) did not differ on any test from 30 people who used other drugs and 30 who used no illicit drugs (Morgan et al., 2009), and the 24 of them retested a year later again showed no deficits (Morgan et al., 2010b); but they were different people from the frequent group and had used less before stopping (2.55 days a month just before stopping and a group peak of 11.21, against the frequent group's 20.13), so these comparisons cannot show recovery, as the authors themselves state. In the only study that retested the same people after they cut down (Morgan et al., 2004a), 18 of the 57 ketamine participants of two earlier field studies (editors' calculation), all of whom had cut down (from a mean of 6.45 to 1.61 days a month; 8 had not used for more than 6 months), were retested 3 to 4 years after a session held 3 days after a night of use, beside 10 polydrug controls: their lower category fluency no longer differed (group × time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032), a gain the authors report as correlated with the reduction in use (r = 0.712); but story recall and digit-cancellation speed (66.01 and 65.32 against 54.60 and 55.97 seconds) were lower at both sessions with no reported change, and sentence judging was lower across both sessions although it appeared to improve, which fits differences that were there before as well as lasting effects, as the authors concede for story recall. People who kept using frequently also improved over a year on spatial working memory (errors 29.58 to 19.92), pattern recognition (83.68% to 89.04%) and planning although their use changed little; the authors attribute the planning and strategy gains partly to practice on tasks with only one version and to a poor start, and their reported correlations between change in amount and change in the other two scores (r = 0.623 and −0.732) are weaker in the plotted points (about 0.55 and −0.55, editors' calculation). Letter fluency fell over the year in the abstinent and frequent groups, and also in both control groups. All the evidence comes from one research group, with self-reported use. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Ex-ketamine group (Morgan et al., 2009; 30 people, abstinent a mean of 344.43 days, range 120–2980; 2.55 days a month before stopping, peak 11.21, against the frequent group's 20.13): no differences from 30 polydrug and 30 non-drug controls on any test; 24 retested a year later: no deficits at either session (Morgan et al., 2010b). Morgan et al. (2004a), 18 who had cut down (6.45 to 1.61 days a month) against 10 polydrug controls, 3–4 years apart: category fluency group × time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032 (first session t = 2.42, P = 0.023; no difference at follow-up); change in category fluency with change in use r = 0.712; story recall group F(1,26) = 4.36 (immediate) and 4.43 (delayed); digit cancellation 66.01 and 65.32 against 54.60 and 55.97 s; sentences judged group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007. Frequent group over a year, still using (Morgan et al., 2010b): errors 29.58 to 19.92; pattern recognition 83.68% to 89.04%; Stockings 7.67 to 9.50; correlations with change in amount r = 0.623 and −0.732 as printed, about 0.55 and −0.55 from the plotted points (editors' calculation).

claims.statement: In people who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London, frequent ketamine use compared with no ketamine use is associated with lower scores on some memory and planning tests, but not on others, when people are tested one to seven days after their last use; people who use ketamine less often did not score lower. Whether ketamine causes the differences is unknown. In the largest comparison (Morgan et al., 2009; five groups of 30, one session at least 24 hours after any drug), people who used ketamine more than four times a week (19 of 30 said daily), tested a mean of 1.6 days after last use (range 1 to 7), made more errors on a spatial working-memory task (about 32 against 11 to 19, editors' reading of a figure), solved fewer planning problems in the fewest moves (7.66 against 8.89 to 9.53) and recognised fewer patterns (about 83% against 90% to 95%, editors' reading of a figure) than each of the other four groups, which included 30 people who used other drugs but not ketamine and 30 who used no illicit drugs; their word recognition was lower too, although the editors could reproduce only one of the reported pairwise differences from the printed table. Story recall, letter and category fluency, a response-inhibition test and memory for which voice spoke a word did not differ, and people who used ketamine less often (a mean of 3.25 days a month, last use a mean of 11.3 days before) and people who had stopped did not differ from the controls on any test. The frequent group had fewer years of education (12.27 against 14.23 to 15.33), a lower reading-test estimate of earlier ability (45.67 against 47.13 to 51.53) and more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 against 1 to 3), none adjusted for, and it was tested so soon after use that withdrawal or other after-effects of recent use cannot be excluded (the authors raise withdrawal). A year later (Morgan et al., 2010b; the same people, 25 of the 30 retested), the frequent group's scores averaged over both sessions were still lower on spatial working memory and pattern recognition, but its errors fell from 29.58 to 19.92 and its pattern recognition rose from 83.68% to 89.04%, close to the controls' 88.41% and 89.58%, and its planning score reached the other groups' range, although 22 of the 25 were still using ketamine at least monthly. Two smaller field studies by the same team, which tested people three days after a night of use, found lower story recall and category fluency, against peers with little or no ketamine use (Curran & Morgan, 2000) and in people who used ketamine more than twice a month against people who used it less (Curran & Monaghan, 2001); the larger study did not find these differences, and its authors suggest the earlier story recall deficits may reflect missed practice in a design that tested people while intoxicated first. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Morgan et al. (2009), 30 per group, frequent group tested 1.6 days (range 1–7) after last use: spatial working-memory errors about 32 against about 11–19 (editors' reading of Figure 1; F(4, 145) = 8.05); strategy 32.73 against 26.53–28.93; Stockings problems in minimum moves 7.66 against 8.89–9.53 (F(4, 145) = 6.58); pattern recognition about 83% against about 90–95% (editors' reading of Figure 2; F(4, 145) = 6.37); word recognition d′ 2.36 against 2.67–2.97 (F(4, 145) = 2.74; only the difference from the ex-ketamine group reproduces, editors' recalculation). No differences: story recall (immediate 8.11–8.32), letter fluency (15.14–17.53), category fluency (14.73–17.27), Hayling test. Infrequent (3.25 days a month) and ex-ketamine groups: no differences from controls. Confounders: education 12.27 against 14.23–15.33 years; spot-the-word 45.67 against 47.13–51.53; family history of mental illness 8 of 30 against 1–3. Morgan et al. (2010b), 25 of 30 frequent retested after 366.6 days: errors 29.58 to 19.92 (other groups 11.48–18.32, then 12.48–15.89); pattern recognition 83.68% to 89.04% (controls 88.41% and 89.58% at follow-up); Stockings 7.67 to 9.50 (others 9.33–9.87 at follow-up). Field studies, 3 days after use: category fluency 14.85 against 19.68 (2000) and 14.06 against 18.95 (2001); story recall 7.75 against 10.18 (2000) and 4.56 against 9.16 (2001).

claims.statement: In people who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London, frequent ketamine use compared with no ketamine use is associated with more delusion-like (unusual) beliefs, more dissociation in everyday life and somewhat more depressive symptoms, mostly below levels the authors regard as clinical; whether ketamine causes these differences is unknown. In one session (Morgan et al., 2009; groups of 30), people who used ketamine more than four times a week scored higher than 30 people who used other drugs and 30 who used no illicit drugs on a delusions inventory (22.72 against 13.03 and 9.43), on unusual experiences in daily life when not under the influence of drugs, on a dissociative experiences scale (784 against 488 and 321) and on a depression inventory (11.48 against 7.17 and 7.23, which the authors call mild to moderate depression); the editors could reproduce the differences from both control groups for delusions and dissociation, but for depression only the difference from the group who had stopped. People who used ketamine less often (at least monthly but less than four times a week) or had stopped scored between the frequent and non-drug groups on several of these scales, but their reported excess of delusional ideation over the non-drug group could not be reproduced from the printed table. A year later (Morgan et al., 2010b; the same people), delusional ideation (8.39 and 8.04 items endorsed in the frequent group, against 5.63 and 4.50 in the polydrug and 3.90 and 3.95 in the non-drug group) and dissociation were still highest in the frequent group, and depression scores had risen in the frequent (7.08 to 10.67) and abstinent groups (4.96 to 9.00). Three days after a night of use, a ketamine group that used ketamine from twice a week to once a month rated more dissociation (17.75 against 5.37) and psychosis-like experiences (62.35 against 26.42) than peers with little or no ketamine use, and slightly higher depression scores on both test days, the first rating covering the two days up to the test on the night (Curran & Morgan, 2000); in a second sample, people who used ketamine more than twice a month and people who used it less did not differ in dissociation or psychosis-like scores three days after use (Curran & Monaghan, 2001). In 18 people who had cut down, retested after 3 to 4 years, psychosis-like (schizotypal) scores stayed higher than in 10 controls (18.67 against 4.0) and depression scores were higher (5.27 against 2.00), while dissociation did not differ (Morgan et al., 2004a). The frequent group of the main study had more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 against 1 to 3) and less education; nobody was assessed before using ketamine, the measures are self-ratings, and no study read gives a rate of diagnosed psychotic illness (one person in the 3-year follow-up had developed schizophrenia and was excluded, a single case that gives no rate). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Morgan et al. (2009), groups of 30: delusions inventory total 22.72 (frequent) against 15.1 (infrequent), 15.79 (ex-ketamine), 13.03 (polydrug) and 9.43 (non-drug); dissociative experiences 784 against 630, 401, 488 and 321; Beck Depression Inventory 11.48 against 9.03, 6.00, 7.17 and 7.23 (only the difference from the ex-ketamine group reproduces, editors' recalculation); delusions with amount per session in the frequent group r = 0.433. Morgan et al. (2010b), same cohort one year later: delusions items 8.39 and 8.04 (frequent) against 5.63 and 4.50 (polydrug) and 3.90 and 3.95 (non-drug); dissociation, frequent above both control groups (P = 0.015 and 0.009); depression 7.08 to 10.67 (frequent) and 4.96 to 9.00 (abstinent). Curran & Morgan (2000), 3 days after use: dissociation 17.75 against 5.37, schizotypal 62.35 against 26.42; HADS depression 4.30 against 1.68 (and 4.45 against 1.89 for the two days up to the night). Curran & Monaghan (2001), 3 days after use: dissociation 4.56 against 3.47, schizotypal 25.28 against 28.95 (no difference). Morgan et al. (2004a), 18 against 10: schizotypal 51.5 against 24.8 and 18.67 against 4.0; dissociation 10.11 against 5.44 and 3.24 against 0.80 (no difference); HADS depression at follow-up 5.27 against 2.00.
